newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House prepares to vote on Gingrich reprimand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House prepares to vote on Gingrich reprimand.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives will vote on a proposal on Tuesday to reprimand Newt Gingrich and "fine" him $300,000 for violating House rules, climaxing two years of bitter partisan squabbling over the controversial speaker.

Both Democrats and Republicans predicted the House, voting after a scheduled one-hour debate, would overwhelmingly support the severe penalty adopted by its ethics committee on Friday by a vote of 7-1, and accepted by Gingrich.

The House vote comes one day after President Bill Clinton, in his inaugural address at the start of his second term, called for an end to partisan bickering, echoing hopes expressed by members of both parties.

After the Gingrich vote "we get a fresh start," Republican Conference Chairman John Boehner of Ohio said on Sunday. "We begin to deal with what the American people sent us here to do, balance the budget, cut taxes, solve the problems of Medicare."
California Democrat Vic Fazio said he hoped the vote would mark the end of the controversy that surrounded the Gingrich affair and split the ethics committee chaired by Republican Nancy Johnson.

Gingrich himself sounded a conciliatory theme when he made a lighthearted address at a congressional lunch after Clinton's inaugural ceremony, saying he found "a sense of bipartisan excitement" at the event.

Gingrich, who was re-elected speaker only 13 days ago, was not expected to be in the House chamber on Tuesday when he becomes the first sitting speaker ever to be reprimanded. The speaker is the third highest elected official of the United States after the president and vice president.

The punishment was for bringing discredit on the House by giving false statements to the ethics committee and failing to seek legal advice on use of tax-free charitable contributions for partisan political purposes.
The ethics committee said the offence called for a penalty "somewhere in between" a reprimand and the more serious censure, which would have almost certainly required Gingrich to step down.

The $300,000 "fine" was to meet some of the costs the committee incurred as a result of Gingrich's false statements. A spokeswoman for Gingrich said on Monday that no decision had yet been made on how the money is to be paid.
Recent public opinion polls have suggested Gingrich is one of the most unpopular politicians in the United States, with only about a third of Americans approving of the job he is doing.
